poultry-fish.factor: White meat, red meat and processed meat
poultry-fish.originalClaim: Original action section: white meat −11% to −3% ACM; evidence section: increasing red meat by ≥half a serving/day increases ACM by 10%; two servings of red/processed meat per week increases it by 3%.
poultry-fish.finding: The original paragraph combines two papers: JAMA on an additional 2 servings of meat per week and BMJ on eight-year changes in red meat intake. No significant white-meat association with ACM does not establish absence of risk; poultry was associated with higher CVD risk in JAMA.
poultry-fish.effect: Processed meat HR 1.03; red meat HR 1.03; poultry HR 0.99; fish HR 0.99; red meat increase ≥half a serving/day HR 1.10
poultry-fish.comparison: JAMA: each additional 2 servings/week; BMJ: increase ≥half a serving/day over eight years versus stable intake
poultry-fish.population: JAMA: 29,682 participants in 6 US cohorts, 8,875 deaths; BMJ: 81,469 participants, 14,019 deaths
poultry-fish.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
poultry-fish.limitations: Food questionnaires and residual confounding; different exposure time windows in the two studies
poultry-fish.action: Limit processed meat; replace some red meat with legumes, nuts, fish and similar foods. Consider cooking methods and the overall diet.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: ACM estimates for processed meat 1.03 (1.02–1.05), red meat 1.03 (1.01–1.05), poultry 0.99 (0.97–1.02), fish 0.99 (0.97–1.01).
Abstract, Results: eight-year intake changes and deaths over the following eight years; HR 1.10 (1.04–1.17).

fresh-fruit-diabetes.originalClaim: Eating 200 g of fresh fruit daily can reduce mortality by 17%, diabetic macrovascular complications by 13% and microvascular complications by 28%.
fresh-fruit-diabetes.finding: The originally cited conference abstract on global CVD-attributable burden is not the source of this ACM figure. The actual source is the CKB diabetes population: per additional 100 g/day, rather than 200 g, ACM HR 0.83; macrovascular 0.87 and microvascular 0.72 also refer to each 100 g/day. This cannot be generalized to a 17% reduction from 200 g/day for everyone.
fresh-fruit-diabetes.comparison: Each additional 100 g/day of fresh fruit in people with diabetes
fresh-fruit-diabetes.population: China CKB: 30,300 participants with diabetes at baseline, 3,389 deaths, about 7 years
fresh-fruit-diabetes.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
fresh-fruit-diabetes.limitations: Specific diabetes population; nonrandomized; mismatch between the cited endpoint and dose
fresh-fruit-diabetes.action: Replace desserts with moderate amounts of whole fruit, adjusted to blood glucose and the individual treatment plan; do not substitute fruit juice.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods and findings: 30,300 participants with diabetes at baseline; per 100 g/day, ACM HR 0.83 (0.74–0.93), microvascular 0.72 (0.61–0.87), macrovascular 0.87 (0.82–0.93).

Bibliographic details checked only: conference abstract on global/regional/national cardiovascular disease burden related to fruit and vegetables. Main text not obtained; not used as quantitative ACM evidence.

flavonoid-foods.originalClaim: Eating flavonoid-containing foods is associated with 20% lower mortality risk; examples include a cup of tea, an apple, an orange, 100 g of blueberries or 100 g of broccoli.
flavonoid-foods.finding: The direction of association is supported, but this was not a trial of 100 g of broccoli daily. The association levels off around total flavonoid intake of 500 mg/day. After further dietary adjustment, Q3 HR was 0.88 and Q5 HR 0.92; a blanket 20% reduction ignores model differences.
flavonoid-foods.comparison: Total flavonoid intake quintiles 3/5 versus quintile 1, Table 2 Model 3
flavonoid-foods.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
flavonoid-foods.limitations: Confounding by healthy diet and socioeconomic factors; single FFQ; supplement effects cannot be inferred
flavonoid-foods.action: Obtain plant nutrients from varied vegetables, fruit, legumes and similar foods; do not rely on flavonoid supplements or use them to offset smoking or alcohol.

sources.evidence: Full text, Table 2, total flavonoids: Model 2 Q3/Q5 both about 0.83; Model 3 Q3 0.88 (0.84–0.91), Q5 0.92 (0.88–0.97). Results: plateau around 500 mg/day.

chili-us.originalClaim: US study of 16,179 people followed for about 19 years: deaths in 21.6% of chili consumers versus 33.6% of nonconsumers; the original paragraph then claims 23% lower ACM with >4 times/week.
chili-us.finding: The 16,179 participants, 4,946 deaths and 21.6% versus 33.6% are from the US study. Adjusted ACM was 13% lower, distinct from the crude risk difference and the Italian 23% estimate.
chili-us.comparison: Hot red chili pepper consumption versus none
chili-us.population: US NHANES III: 16,179 adults, median 18.9 years
chili-us.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
chili-us.limitations: Crude death proportions are confounded by age and other factors; single dietary measurement
chili-us.action: Use as seasoning if enjoyed and tolerated; people with gastrointestinal discomfort need not force an increase.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: US NHANES III, 16,179 participants, 4,946 deaths, median 18.9 years; consumers versus nonconsumers, adjusted HR 0.87 (0.77–0.97); crude death proportions 21.6% versus 33.6%.

chili-italy.originalClaim: Eating chili >4 times/week reduces ACM by 23% and cardiovascular mortality by 34%; a secondary headline claims “61% lower risk of illness-related death.”
chili-italy.finding: The associations of >4 times/week with 23% lower ACM and 34% lower CVD mortality come from the Italian cohort. The 61% refers to a relative reduction in cerebrovascular mortality, not overall illness-related mortality. The reference was never/rare consumption, not everyone consuming chili fewer than 2 times/week.
chili-italy.population: Italian Moli-sani cohort: 22,811 participants, 1,236 deaths, median 8.2 years
chili-italy.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
chili-italy.limitations: Residual dietary/lifestyle confounding; does not establish efficacy of a capsaicin intervention
chili-italy.action: Eat according to tolerance; this cannot replace blood pressure control or other treatment.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: Italian Moli-sani, 22,811 participants, 1,236 deaths, median 8.2 years; >4 times/week versus never/rarely: ACM HR 0.77 (0.66–0.90), CVD mortality 0.66 (0.50–0.86), cerebrovascular mortality 0.39 (0.20–0.75).

eggs.originalClaim: An additional half an egg daily increases all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk by 7%; replacing half a whole egg with egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy, nuts or legumes gives modeled ACM reductions of 6%, 8%, 9%, 7%, 13% and 10%.
eggs.finding: The original 7% and substitution-model figures were verified. These are observational results in middle-aged and older US adults and hypothetical equivalent-amount substitutions, not mortality reductions caused by randomized dietary changes, nor a fixed 7% increase from eggs for everyone.
eggs.effect: HR 1.07 per additional half a whole egg/day
eggs.comparison: Each additional 25 g/day of whole egg; substitution model, not an actual intervention
eggs.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
eggs.limitations: Self-report, single baseline diet measurement, residual confounding; results may differ across regions
eggs.action: Choose egg intake in the context of overall diet and blood lipids; legumes or nuts can replace some animal protein. Do not eliminate eggs solely on one study.

sources.evidence: Full-text abstract and Results/Hypothetical substitution: half an egg/day, ACM 1.07 (1.06–1.08); replacement with egg whites/poultry/fish/dairy/nuts/legumes respectively gave modeled ACM reductions of 6/8/9/7/13/10%.

walnuts.originalClaim: ≥5 servings of walnuts/week (28 g/serving): 1.3 more years of healthy life expectancy, 14% lower ACM and 25% lower cardiovascular mortality.
walnuts.finding: 14% lower ACM with ≥5 servings/week is supported. The 1.30/1.26 years are modeled total life expectancy at age 60, not healthy life expectancy or a guarantee of longer life.
walnuts.comparison: ≥5 servings/week versus none; 28 g per serving
walnuts.population: NHS/HPFS: 93,340 participants, 30,263 deaths, up to 20 years
walnuts.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
walnuts.limitations: Healthy-user bias; modeled life expectancy; industry funding warrants attention
walnuts.action: If not allergic to nuts, replace snacks with moderate amounts of unsalted nuts, accounting for total energy intake.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: ≥5 servings/week HR 0.86 (0.79–0.93); life expectancy at age 60 was 1.30 years longer for women and 1.26 for men, not healthy life expectancy.

nuts-general.originalClaim: The original describes weekly frequency using a 1-ounce serving, with mortality reductions of 7%, 11%, 13%, 15% and 20%; it also calls a 7,216-person study “cross-sectional,” reporting 39% lower mortality with >3 servings/week.
nuts-general.finding: NEJM frequencies were <1, 1, 2–4, 5–6 and ≥7 times/week, corresponding to 7/11/13/15/20% lower mortality, not groups based on total weekly weight; these data do not establish that nuts must be eaten raw. The PREDIMED 39% comes from an observational analysis of nut intake, neither cross-sectional nor the ACM effect of separately randomized nut intake.
nuts-general.effect: NEJM ≥7 times/week HR 0.80; PREDIMED >3 servings/week HR 0.61
nuts-general.population: NEJM: 118,962 participants, 27,429 deaths; PREDIMED: 7,216 adults at high CVD risk, 323 deaths
nuts-general.design: Prospective cohorts and observational analysis within an RCT
nuts-general.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
nuts-general.limitations: Intake groups were not randomized; raw versus roasted nuts not directly tested
nuts-general.action: Avoid if allergic; choose unsalted nuts with little added sugar to replace other energy-dense snacks.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: frequencies <1/1/2–4/5–6/≥7 times/week, respective HRs 0.93/0.89/0.87/0.85/0.80; highest-group CI 0.73–0.86.
Abstract, Methods/Results: baseline intake and repeated annual measurements associated with mortality; >3 servings/week HR 0.61 (0.45–0.83), 323 deaths.

sodium-ecological.factor: Cross-country ecological association with sodium intake
sodium-ecological.originalClaim: Ecological study of 181 countries: per additional 1 g/day of sodium, healthy life expectancy at birth β=2.6 years and at age 60 β=0.3 years; ACM β=−131; in 46 high-income countries, β=3.4 years and ACM β=−168.
sodium-ecological.finding: The original β values agree with the abstract, but country-level ecological correlations cannot justify individuals eating more salt. The authors explicitly state these data should not be used for nutritional interventions.
sodium-ecological.effect: β −131 death events per 1 g/day higher sodium intake (country-level regression)
sodium-ecological.comparison: Mean sodium intake versus age-standardized mortality measures across 181 countries; not an individual HR
sodium-ecological.population: Aggregated 2010 data from 181 countries; sensitivity analysis in 46 high-income countries
sodium-ecological.gradeReason: Animal, ecological or non-ACM outcomes cannot directly establish individual human ACM effects
sodium-ecological.limitations: Ecological fallacy; confounding by national income and health care; errors in estimated intake
sodium-ecological.action: Do not increase sodium to extend life; manage salt according to personal blood pressure, diseases and diet.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods and results: 181 countries; ACM β −131, R² 0.60, P<0.001; final conclusion states that these observational data should not be used as a basis for nutritional interventions.

potassium-salt.originalClaim: Multiple studies suggest low-sodium salt can reduce disease occurrence and have a positive effect on reducing ACM.
potassium-salt.finding: SSaSS directly supports lower ACM when specific high-risk rural adults replace regular salt with 75% NaCl/25% KCl salt; the separate contributions of sodium reduction and potassium supplementation cannot be isolated.
potassium-salt.comparison: 75% NaCl + 25% KCl versus 100% NaCl; 39.28 versus 44.61 per 1,000 person-years
potassium-salt.population: 20,995 people in 600 Chinese villages; history of stroke or age ≥60 with hypertension; mean follow-up 4.74 years
potassium-salt.design: Open-label cluster-randomized trial; ACM was a secondary endpoint
potassium-salt.gradeReason: Large randomized trial with a direct ACM endpoint; clearly bounded population applicability
potassium-salt.limitations: Specific high-risk population; open-label; limited applicability in kidney disease or risk of hyperkalemia
potassium-salt.action: Suitable people, including those with hypertension, may substitute potassium-enriched lower-sodium salt after confirmation by a health professional. With impaired kidney function, hyperkalemia or potassium-raising medicines, seek advice first rather than changing salt independently.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods/Results: 20,995 participants, 4.74 years; ACM rates 39.28 versus 44.61 per 1,000 person-years, rate ratio 0.88 (0.82–0.95); clinical hyperkalemia 1.04 (0.80–1.37).

carbohydrate-share.originalClaim: Lower carbohydrate intake means shorter life; higher intake also slightly shortens life; about 50% of energy is the longest-life range.
carbohydrate-share.finding: The 2018 study supports a U-shaped observational association, lowest around 50–55% of energy. This does not mean low carbohydrate intake inevitably shortens an individual’s life; the sources of fat/protein replacing carbohydrate matter.
carbohydrate-share.effect: Low carbohydrate HR 1.20; high carbohydrate HR 1.23
carbohydrate-share.comparison: <40% and >70% of energy from carbohydrate, each versus moderate intake (meta-analysis categories); ARIC minimum at 50–55%
carbohydrate-share.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
carbohydrate-share.limitations: Observational and self-reported; differences in intake categories and replacement foods; life expectancy estimates are not interventions
carbohydrate-share.action: Prioritize carbohydrate quality and increase whole grains and legumes; diabetes or therapeutic ketogenic diets require individualization.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Findings: ARIC 15,428 participants and synthesis totaling 432,179; lowest ACM around 50%–55% of energy from carbohydrate; low-carbohydrate HR 1.20 (1.09–1.32), high-carbohydrate 1.23 (1.11–1.36); animal versus plant replacement sources differed in direction.

betel-quid.originalClaim: Chewing areca nut increases all-cause mortality by 21%.
betel-quid.finding: The 21% higher ACM is a pooled relative risk from observational studies. Heterogeneity is high; quid ingredients and co-exposure to tobacco and alcohol affect interpretation.
betel-quid.population: ACM analysis: 179,582 participants, 5 comparison categories in Asian studies
betel-quid.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
betel-quid.limitations: I² 85%; product formulations and residual confounding by smoking/alcohol; nonrandomized
betel-quid.action: Avoid or stop areca/betel-quid use; absence of tobacco does not make it safe. Seek cessation support for dependence.

sources.evidence: Full text, All-cause mortality: 5 comparison categories, N=179,582, RR 1.21 (1.04–1.42), I² 85%, heterogeneity P<0.001.

calorie-restriction.originalClaim: Calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys: normally fed controls had 2.9-fold disease risk and 3.0-fold mortality risk.
calorie-restriction.finding: The original threefold mortality figure concerned age-related deaths in an earlier rhesus-monkey study, not human ACM. The 2014 update from the same project reported all-cause control/CR HR 1.78 and age-related mortality HR 2.89. The magnitude of human life extension is unproven.
calorie-restriction.comparison: Normal feeding versus approximately 30% calorie restriction
calorie-restriction.population: UW: 76 rhesus monkeys; the separate NIA monkey study initially found no significant survival difference
calorie-restriction.gradeReason: Animal, ecological or non-ACM outcomes cannot directly establish individual human ACM effects
calorie-restriction.limitations: Animal results cannot be extrapolated to humans; centers differed in feed, age and control intake
calorie-restriction.action: Avoid overeating while maintaining adequate nutrition. People who are underweight, pregnant/breastfeeding, minors, frail older adults or those with eating disorders should not restrict calories independently.

sources.evidence: Europe PMC original-study abstract (Methods/Results/Findings); original JSON saved: 2009 abstract describes a 20-year animal study with fewer age-related deaths, not human ACM.
Full text, Results: ACM control/CR HR 1.78 (1.04–3.04), P=0.037; age-related HR 2.89 (1.34–6.25); Introduction distinguishes the earlier 3.0-fold mortality figure.

macronutrient-pattern.originalClaim: The original claims universally optimal proportions: <24% starch, 15%–17% protein, >15% monounsaturated fat, <15% sugar, 6% saturated and 6% polyunsaturated fat, and 30 g+ fiber; it also describes a linear association between total fat and ACM.
macronutrient-pattern.finding: Total fat was not significantly associated with ACM in the paper; it did not show all fat to be linearly harmful. The risk matrix describes combinations in observational data, not a universal optimum. Minima on individual nutrient curves included fiber 15–30 g/day, protein 14–18% and starch 20–30%, differing from several original ranges and the precise “optimal proportions.”
macronutrient-pattern.effect: Examples: fiber 15–30 g/day HR 0.68; protein 14–18% HR 0.73
macronutrient-pattern.comparison: Fiber versus 5 g/day; protein versus 10% of energy; each nutrient has its own reference
macronutrient-pattern.population: UK Biobank: 195,658 participants, 4,780 deaths, mean 10.6 years
macronutrient-pattern.design: Large prospective cohort with nonlinear modeling
macronutrient-pattern.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
macronutrient-pattern.limitations: Self-reported 24-hour recalls, selection bias and residual confounding; combining the minima of separate curves does not create a validated prescription
macronutrient-pattern.action: Build a diet around overall food quality rather than exact macronutrient ratios; follow medical nutrition plans for kidney disease, diabetes and similar conditions.

sources.evidence: Full text, Results/Fig 1: total fat not significant; fiber 15–30 g/day versus 5 g/day HR 0.68 (0.65–0.72); protein 14–18% versus 10% HR 0.73 (0.70–0.75). Methods: risk-matrix categories were not randomized dietary comparisons.

ultraprocessed-acm.originalClaim: Original action section: eat fewer ultra-processed foods, −62% to −18%; cited headline claims frequent consumers of chips, burgers and chocolate have an “average age at death of only 58.”
ultraprocessed-acm.finding: SUN supports an association of the highest consumption group with 62% higher ACM. The 58 years is the sample’s mean age among those who died; it does not mean frequent consumers have a life expectancy of 58 or that UPF caused their deaths.
ultraprocessed-acm.comparison: Highest versus lowest quartile; highest group >4 servings/day
ultraprocessed-acm.population: Spanish SUN university graduates: 19,899 participants, 335 deaths, 200,432 person-years
ultraprocessed-acm.gradeReason: Single cohort or substantial confounding/heterogeneity; limited direct ACM evidence
ultraprocessed-acm.limitations: Only 335 deaths; selected highly educated sample; dietary confounding; wide CI
ultraprocessed-acm.action: Replace some UPF with less processed whole foods while preserving adequate nutrition and affordability.

sources.evidence: Full text, Results: 335 deaths; mean age at death 58.0 (SD 15.6); highest/lowest group HR 1.62 (1.13–2.33); per serving HR 1.18 (1.05–1.33).

ultraprocessed-cvd.factor: Ultra-processed foods (endpoint limits of CVD sources)
ultraprocessed-cvd.originalClaim: The ultra-processed food entry lists the SUN all-cause mortality study, the NutriNet-Santé cardiovascular incidence study and a commentary together.
ultraprocessed-cvd.finding: The NutriNet-Santé study examined incident CVD, not ACM. Lawrence/Baker is a commentary with no independent quantitative ACM evidence. These should not be counted with SUN as three mortality studies.
ultraprocessed-cvd.comparison: Each 10-percentage-point increase in the dietary share of UPF
ultraprocessed-cvd.population: France: 105,159 adults, 1,409 CVD events, median 5.2 years
ultraprocessed-cvd.gradeReason: Animal, ecological or non-ACM outcomes cannot directly establish individual human ACM effects
ultraprocessed-cvd.limitations: Non-ACM endpoint; original commentary PDF could not be accessed, bibliographic details only checked
ultraprocessed-cvd.action: These may support an overall dietary direction of reducing UPF, but cannot be used to calculate mortality risk from this paper.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Main outcome/Results: incident CVD, HR 1.12 (1.05–1.20) per 10-percentage-point increase in UPF share; no ACM reported.
Europe PMC bibliographic record PMID 31142449: Ultra-processed food and adverse health outcomes, 2019, BMJ l2289; no abstract, original RG link returned 403; commentary full text not read.

whole-grains.originalClaim: This factor was not in the original repository.
whole-grains.finding: Higher whole-grain intake is associated with lower ACM. The study measures the weight of whole-grain foods; 90 g does not mean 90 g of dry grain or fiber.
whole-grains.comparison: Each additional 90 g/day of whole-grain foods (about 3 servings)
whole-grains.population: 11 prospective studies pooled for ACM; 45 studies in the overall review
whole-grains.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
whole-grains.limitations: ACM I² 83%; observational; heterogeneous food-serving definitions
whole-grains.action: Gradually replace refined grains with whole grains. People with celiac disease should choose gluten-free whole grains; adjust to digestive tolerance.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: ACM per 90 g/day RR 0.83 (0.77–0.90), I² 83%, 11 studies; the 90 g example is two slices of bread and a bowl of cereal.

dietary-fiber.originalClaim: This factor was not in the original repository.
dietary-fiber.finding: The review supports an association between higher fiber intake and lower ACM. The abstract’s 15–30% range covers multiple outcomes, not a precise ACM-specific effect. RCTs demonstrated improvements in risk factors rather than reduced deaths.
dietary-fiber.effect: Direction of ACM association: lower; the abstract gives no separate precise pooled ACM estimate
dietary-fiber.comparison: Highest versus lowest fiber consumption; 15–30% lower risk across several outcomes
dietary-fiber.population: 185 prospective studies and 58 trials; 4,635 trial participants
dietary-fiber.design: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (ACM from cohorts)
dietary-fiber.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
dietary-fiber.limitations: Nonrandomized ACM evidence; do not derive an ACM CI from the overall range
dietary-fiber.action: Gradually increase fiber from whole grains, legumes, vegetables and fruit, with attention to fluid intake; follow medical advice for intestinal narrowing or acute gastrointestinal disease.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Findings: 185 cohorts, 58 clinical trials; observational data showed 15–30% reductions across several outcomes, with greater benefits around 25–29 g/day. Trials reported weight/blood pressure/cholesterol, not ACM.

plant-protein.originalClaim: This factor was not in the original repository.
plant-protein.finding: Higher plant protein intake is associated with lower ACM. The foods being replaced matter; this cannot be interpreted as an intervention effect of adding protein powder.
plant-protein.comparison: Highest versus lowest plant protein intake
plant-protein.design: Systematic review/dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts
plant-protein.gradeReason: Direct ACM associations from pooled cohorts or a large, high-quality cohort; not proof of causation
plant-protein.limitations: Heterogeneity I² 57.5%; residual confounding; difficult to separate whole-food effects from protein components
plant-protein.action: Replace some red/processed meat with legumes, soy foods and nuts; adjust for allergies or kidney disease according to individual needs.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: plant protein and ACM, pooled effect size 0.92 (0.87–0.97), I² 57.5%; each additional 3% of energy was associated with 5% lower ACM; the abstract gives no CI for that dose estimate.

dairy.originalClaim:
* Milk
  * [The Lancet study of 130,000 people in 21 countries: 500 g of milk or yogurt daily lowers cardiovascular mortality risk by 23%](https://www.sohu.com/a/253940257_419768)
  * Source: [Association of dairy intake with cardiovascular disease and mortality in 21 countries from five continents (PURE): a prospective cohort study](http://mdrf-eprints.in/1114/1/Association_of_dietary_patterns_and_dietary_diversity_with_cardiometabolic_disease_risk_factors.pdf)
  * Compared with people consuming no dairy, those consuming two servings daily (a serving means 244 g of milk/yogurt, 15 g of cheese or 5 g of butter) had **17% lower all-cause mortality risk**, 23% lower cardiovascular mortality risk and 33% lower stroke risk
Original action section: drink milk (−17% to −10% ACM)
dairy.finding: The PURE 17% is an ACM association for >2 servings/day of total dairy versus none, not the effect of milk alone or exactly 2 servings. The 95% CI for cardiovascular mortality HR 0.77 crosses 1, so a 23% decrease cannot be stated as an established benefit. Other reviews found no consistent ACM association for total dairy or milk; milk should not be promised to extend life. The original PDF was inaccessible, and its filename does not match the cited title, suggesting an incorrect link.
dairy.comparison: Total dairy >2 servings/day versus 0; not milk alone
dairy.population: 136,384 people in 21 countries, ages 35–70; median follow-up 9.1 years; 6,796 deaths
dairy.design: PURE prospective cohort; additionally checked a review of 8 meta-analyses
dairy.gradeReason: Large multinational cohort with a direct ACM endpoint; inconsistent results across other pooled cohorts preclude causal inference
dairy.limitations: FFQ error and residual confounding by income and dietary patterns; dairy types and replacement foods matter. HR 0.90 for >1 serving of milk concerns the death/CVD composite, not milk-specific ACM.
dairy.action: Choose milk or yogurt without added sugar according to nutritional needs; use suitable alternatives for lactose intolerance or milk allergy rather than forcing higher intake for longevity.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods/Findings: total dairy >2 servings/day versus none, ACM 0.83 (0.72–0.96); cardiovascular mortality 0.77 (0.58–1.01).
Abstract: 8 meta-analyses; RR range 0.99–1.01 per 200–244 g of milk; conclusion found no ACM association.

tea-china-par.originalClaim:
* Tea
  * [Following 100,000 Chinese people for 7 years found tea three times/week associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality risk and 1.26 years longer life expectancy ](https://www.jianshu.com/p/5461a205cf95?utm_campaign=hugo)
  * Source: [Tea consumption and the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: The China-PAR project](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Fangchao-Liu-4/publication/338483323_Tea_consumption_and_the_risk_of_atherosclerotic_cardiovascular_disease_and_all-cause_mortality_The_China-PAR_project/links/5e55e5e94585152ce8efe511/Tea-consumption-and-the-risk-of-atherosclerotic-cardiovascular-disease-and-all-cause-mortality-The-China-PAR-project.pdf)
  * [Prospective study of tea consumption and mortality risk in Chinese adults](http://rs.yiigle.com/CN112338202202/1351516.htm)
  * Among 438,443 participants analyzed, 34,661 deaths occurred over 11.1 years. Compared with never tea drinkers, current nondaily and daily drinkers had respective all-cause mortality HRs (95% CIs) of 0.89 (0.86–0.91) and 0.92 (0.88–0.95). Sex-stratified analysis showed the protective association mainly in men (interaction P<0.05).
Original action section: drink tea (−15% to −8% ACM)
tea-china-par.finding: Habitual tea drinking is associated with lower ACM; the ≥3 times/week definition comes from the main text. The 1.26-year longer life expectancy at age 50 is modeled, not an intervention showing everyone lives 1.26 years longer by drinking tea.
tea-china-par.design: Pooling of three China-PAR prospective cohorts
tea-china-par.gradeReason: Multiple cohorts and a large sample with direct ACM; direction similar to CKB, but observational
tea-china-par.limitations: Self-reported tea intake; residual confounding by smoking, alcohol, socioeconomic status and health behaviors; cup sizes, strength and tea types are not equivalent; life expectancy difference is modeled.
tea-china-par.action: If enjoyed and tolerated, choose unsweetened tea that is not scalding hot. Reduce intake with insomnia, palpitations or a need to limit caffeine; tea does not replace smoking cessation or treatment.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: ACM 0.85 (0.79–0.90), life expectancy difference at age 50 of 1.26 years; main-text Methods define tea drinking as ≥3 times/week (web-jama-tea-extract.json).

tea-ckb.originalClaim:
* Tea
  * [Following 100,000 Chinese people for 7 years found tea three times/week associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality risk and 1.26 years longer life expectancy ](https://www.jianshu.com/p/5461a205cf95?utm_campaign=hugo)
  * Source: [Tea consumption and the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: The China-PAR project](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Fangchao-Liu-4/publication/338483323_Tea_consumption_and_the_risk_of_atherosclerotic_cardiovascular_disease_and_all-cause_mortality_The_China-PAR_project/links/5e55e5e94585152ce8efe511/Tea-consumption-and-the-risk-of-atherosclerotic-cardiovascular-disease-and-all-cause-mortality-The-China-PAR-project.pdf)
  * [Prospective study of tea consumption and mortality risk in Chinese adults](http://rs.yiigle.com/CN112338202202/1351516.htm)
  * Among 438,443 participants analyzed, 34,661 deaths occurred over 11.1 years. Compared with never tea drinkers, current nondaily and daily drinkers had respective all-cause mortality HRs (95% CIs) of 0.89 (0.86–0.91) and 0.92 (0.88–0.95). Many foods contain substantial amounts, including fresh green peppers, wheat germ, cauliflower, broccoli, mushrooms and various cheeses; levels are especially high in soy products such as natto, shiitake mushrooms and durian. Researchers followed 829 participants aged 45–84 for 20 years to analyze the potential association between dietary spermidine intake and human mortality.

spermidine-diet.finding: The two duplicate original entries are merged. The exposure was dietary intake, not medication or a liquid; 40.5, 23.7 and 15.1 are deaths per 1,000 person-years, not percentages. The independent SAPHIR cohort supported the direction, but overall food quality cannot be separated from spermidine itself.
spermidine-diet.effect: HR 0.76 per 1 SD higher dietary intake
spermidine-diet.comparison: Each additional 1 SD of continuous dietary intake; not a supplement RCT
spermidine-diet.population: Bruneck: 829 people aged 45–84; 341 deaths in 1995–2015; independent SAPHIR validation

spermidine-diet.gradeReason: Dietary observational ACM evidence with a small primary cohort and dietary confounding; no direct supplement longevity trial

spermidine-diet.action: Obtain it through ordinary balanced foods such as whole grains and legumes; do not buy or take spermidine on a “60% lower mortality” claim. People with medical conditions should check supplements with a clinician.

smoking.originalClaim:

During follow-up, all-cause mortality hazard ratios versus never smoking were 1.17 (95% CI 1.10–1.25) for <10 cigarettes/day and 1.54 (1.42–1.67) for ≥10/day, similar across ages and sexes.   * [Why is smoking addictive? Is smoking in moderation still harmful?](https://www.zhihu.com/question/24846224/answer/1719798177)

The original 11–12 years was not verified from the Mexican paper; populations with differing smoking intensity cannot be combined into one uniform estimate.

sun-exposure.population: Denmark: 4.4 million people aged >40, 1980–2006; Sweden: 29,518 women followed for 20 years

sun-exposure.action: Regular outdoor activity and natural light are reasonable while avoiding sunburn and tanning beds. Follow medical sun-protection advice with photosensitive disease, relevant medicines or high skin cancer risk.
