glucosamine-chondroitin.finding: The original 39% lower ACM and 65% lower CVD mortality are age-adjusted only. Fully adjusted HRs were 0.73 for ACM (27% lower) and 0.42 for CVD (58% lower). Persistent users numbered 658, not 648. These are observational associations, not direct proof of efficacy “equivalent to exercise” or an effective longevity dose of 500–1,000 mg.
glucosamine-chondroitin.comparison: Baseline reported glucosamine/chondroitin use for ≥365 days versus nonuse or <365 days
glucosamine-chondroitin.population: NHANES 1999–2010: 16,686 adults aged ≥40, excluding baseline CVD and missing vital status; 658 users for ≥1 year; median 107 months; 3,366 deaths
glucosamine-chondroitin.design: Mortality follow-up analysis of a national cohort
glucosamine-chondroitin.gradeReason: Small exposed group with substantial healthy-user bias and confounding; no longevity RCT
glucosamine-chondroitin.limitations: Age-adjusted and multivariable-adjusted estimates cannot be interchanged; combined supplements cannot establish a glucosamine-only effect; baseline self-reported use, with no follow-up dose or adherence tracking. Users exercised more, smoked less and were more educated; adjustment cannot eliminate healthy-user or other-supplement confounding.
glucosamine-chondroitin.action: Do not start glucosamine/chondroitin for longevity. With joint symptoms or anticoagulant treatment, discuss suitability and interactions with a clinician; continue regular exercise.

sources.evidence: This round read the original journal Methods (Study Participants / Glucosamine/Chondroitin Use), Results and Discussion: age ≥40; ≥365 days of use versus nonuse or <365 days; 658 users; age-adjusted ACM 0.61 (0.49–0.77), CVD 0.35 (0.20–0.61); multivariable-adjusted ACM 0.73 (0.57–0.93), CVD 0.42 (0.23–0.75); dose and adherence during follow-up were not tracked.

anti-aging-drugs-review.originalClaim:
* Overview
  * [Nature-family in-depth review: developing anti-aging drugs](https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/145495570)
  * ![Developing anti-aging drugs](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2707039/163702474-205baeec-f0ce-4e8d-96a4-36efe47534de.jpg)
anti-aging-drugs-review.finding: The corresponding 2020 Nature Reviews Drug Discovery review discusses rapamycin, senolytics, metformin, acarbose, spermidine, NAD enhancers, lithium and others. Its tiers primarily reflect preclinical and some clinical findings; it is not a meta-analysis demonstrating reduced ACM in healthy people.
anti-aging-drugs-review.effect: No pooled ACM effect applicable to healthy people reported
anti-aging-drugs-review.comparison: Mechanistic, animal and early clinical studies of different candidates; no common randomized ACM comparator
anti-aging-drugs-review.population: Mainly animal models and limited human studies; not a mortality-intervention population of healthy people
anti-aging-drugs-review.gradeReason: Only indirect evidence for healthy-person ACM; journal prestige does not raise the grade
anti-aging-drugs-review.limitations: Different molecules, doses and indications cannot be combined as an “anti-aging drug regimen”; disease-indication benefit does not mean healthy-person life extension. Review dates to 2020, not a comprehensive search of all new drugs through 2026.
anti-aging-drugs-review.action: Do not independently combine anti-aging drugs. Treat clear disease indications under specialist care; experimental anti-aging interventions belong in properly conducted research.

sources.evidence: Abstract: candidates divided into two tiers based on preclinical and some clinical evidence, aiming to extend healthspan; no human healthy-person ACM efficacy reported.

alcohol.originalClaim: Original action section: quit alcohol (otherwise approximately +50% ACM, with no upper limit); section 6 has no corresponding evidence entry.
alcohol.finding: An original systematic review was added to address the action section’s missing citation. After adjustment for former-drinker bias and other factors, low-volume drinking had no significant protective ACM association. At 45 to <65 g ethanol/day RR was 1.19, and at ≥65 g/day 1.35. Any alcohol consumption cannot uniformly be described as “about +50% with no upper limit”; no significant low-volume ACM benefit also does not establish any dose as absolutely safe.
alcohol.comparison: Categories of mean daily ethanol grams versus lifetime nondrinkers
alcohol.gradeReason: Multiple cohorts with direct ACM; addresses some key biases but cannot eliminate confounding
alcohol.limitations: Underreported intake, illness among former drinkers, binge patterns, sex differences and study-level meta-regression limits; risk appeared at lower intake in women. Not a cessation intervention trial, so it cannot directly quantify cessation benefit.
alcohol.action: Nondrinkers should not start for health. Drinkers should reduce total intake and binge drinking. With alcohol dependence or withdrawal history, seek medical support and avoid abrupt unsupported cessation.

sources.evidence: Full text, Results and Table 2, fully adjusted: low-volume 0.93 (0.85–1.01), 45–<65 g/day 1.19 (1.07–1.32), ≥65 g/day 1.35 (1.23–1.47); XML and text saved.

ambient-air-pollution.originalClaim: Not listed in the original repository; added in this round.
ambient-air-pollution.finding: In a large Medicare cohort, each 10 μg/m³ higher long-term PM2.5 was associated with 7.3% higher ACM; each 10 ppb higher ozone with 1.1% higher ACM. These are environmental exposure associations, not equivalent mortality reductions from using a particular air purifier.
ambient-air-pollution.effect: ACM risk increase 7.3% per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5
ambient-air-pollution.comparison: Each 10 μg/m³ higher residentially estimated annual PM2.5; two-pollutant model
ambient-air-pollution.gradeReason: High-quality, exceptionally large direct-ACM cohort; nonrandomized, with exposure-estimation and individual-confounding limits
ambient-air-pollution.limitations: Older US population; ZIP-code exposure is not individual inhalation; lacks detailed individual smoking and similar data; association does not directly quantify a personal air-cleaning intervention effect.
ambient-air-pollution.action: Monitor local air quality; during high pollution, reduce strenuous outdoor activity at high-exposure times and improve indoor air where feasible. Balance ventilation with pollution and infection conditions.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5, ACM increase 7.3% (7.1%–7.5%); per 10 ppb ozone, increase 1.1% (1.0%–1.2%).

statins-indicated-patients.factor: Statins (according to cardiovascular risk and indications)
statins-indicated-patients.originalClaim: Not listed in the original repository; added in this round.
statins-indicated-patients.finding: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials found ACM RR 0.91 per 1 mmol/L lower LDL-C among people without prior vascular disease. This applies to trial participants suitable for lipid-lowering treatment, not medication for every healthy person; absolute benefit depends on baseline risk.
statins-indicated-patients.effect: RR 0.91 per 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction (no prior vascular disease)
statins-indicated-patients.comparison: Statin versus control or more versus less intensive treatment; standardized to LDL-C difference
statins-indicated-patients.population: 27 RCTs, 174,149 people; ACM figure is for the no-prior-vascular-disease subgroup; median 4.8–5.1 years
statins-indicated-patients.gradeReason: Pooled randomized direct-ACM evidence; explicit subgroup, standardized exposure and clinically eligible population
statins-indicated-patients.limitations: Includes primary and secondary prevention; 0.91 is the no-history subgroup. Absolute benefits differ by risk. Local 2026 prescribing thresholds were not separately checked; this entry is not a basis for self-prescribing.
statins-indicated-patients.action: Discuss statins with a clinician if you have ASCVD or meet assessed lipid-lowering indications. Low-risk healthy people should not start solely for “longevity”; muscle symptoms, interactions and pregnancy require individual assessment.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Findings: without prior vascular disease, per 1 mmol/L lower LDL-C, ACM RR 0.91 (0.85–0.97); major vascular events RR 0.79 (0.77–0.81), a distinct endpoint.

vitamin-d-general-population.originalClaim: Not listed in the original repository; added in this round.
vitamin-d-general-population.finding: VITAL found no ACM reduction with 2,000 IU/day vitamin D3: HR 0.99, CI crossing 1. This does not negate treatment of deficiency, bone disease or other clear indications, nor prove all doses completely safe long term.
vitamin-d-general-population.population: US: 25,871 people, men ≥50 and women ≥55; median 5.3 years; 978 deaths
vitamin-d-general-population.gradeReason: Direct large randomized ACM outcome; secondary ACM endpoint and smaller effects cannot be excluded; grade does not mean longevity efficacy
vitamin-d-general-population.limitations: Not selected for severe deficiency; most were not deficient, and results do not cover all doses/indications. Observational low-vitamin-D associations do not establish causal supplementation effects.
vitamin-d-general-population.action: Do not blindly take high doses for longevity; suspected deficiency or clear indications such as bone health warrant clinician-guided supplementation.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: 978 all-cause deaths; vitamin D versus placebo HR 0.99 (0.87–1.12); 25,871 randomized, median 5.3 years.

racquet-sports.originalClaim: Racquet sports 3 times/week for 45–60 minutes/session reduce ACM by about 47%; the cited headline attributes this to The Lancet.
racquet-sports.finding: 47% corresponds to the adjusted ACM hazard ratio in racquet-sport participants, not a randomized intervention effect. The abstract does not support the exact prescription of three 45–60-minute sessions/week or establish the best value among all sports. The paper appeared in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, not The Lancet.
racquet-sports.comparison: Racquet-sport participation versus no participation in that sport category
racquet-sports.gradeReason: Large population cohort with direct ACM; still a noncausal association
racquet-sports.limitations: Self-reported activity, healthy-participant and socioeconomic confounding; cannot unconditionally extrapolate to table tennis or every age.
racquet-sports.action: Choose enjoyable racquet activities compatible with your physical condition and increase gradually; seek assessment for joint injuries or cardiovascular symptoms.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods/Results: n=80,306; racquet sports ACM HR 0.53 (0.40–0.69), CVD mortality HR 0.44 (0.24–0.83).

vigorous-activity.originalClaim: 15–20 minutes/week of vigorous activity reduces ACM by 16%–40%; reaching 50–57 minutes can reduce it further.
vigorous-activity.finding: The original labels the paper’s 16–40% range across mortality endpoints as all ACM. About 15 minutes/week corresponds to 18% lower ACM, about 19.2 minutes to 40% lower cardiovascular mortality, and about 53.6 minutes/week to 36% lower ACM. These are modeled associations relative to 2.2 minutes/week, not guaranteed benefits from 8 minutes daily.
vigorous-activity.comparison: VPA about 15 or 53.6 minutes/week versus 2.2 minutes/week
vigorous-activity.population: 71,893 UK Biobank adults; median age 62.5, mean follow-up 5.9 years
vigorous-activity.design: Wrist-accelerometer prospective cohort with dose-response modeling
vigorous-activity.gradeReason: Large cohort with objective activity measurement and direct ACM endpoint
vigorous-activity.limitations: Nonrandomized; selection bias and residual confounding; the curve minimum is not an optimal prescription for everyone.
vigorous-activity.action: With an exercise foundation and no contraindications, gradually add brief higher-intensity activity. Seek assessment first for symptoms or unstable chronic disease.

sources.evidence: Full-text Abstract and Results, “VPA volume dose–response association”/Figure 4: 1,927 ACM deaths; about 15 minutes HR 0.82, 53.6 minutes HR 0.64; 19.2 minutes HR 0.60 (0.50–0.72) concerns CVD mortality.

walking-steps.originalClaim: Walking reduces all-cause mortality by over 50%; mean participant age was 45.2, and the original notes that this indicates correlation only.
walking-steps.finding: Both 7,000–9,999 and ≥10,000 steps/day were associated with lower ACM, by about 72% and 55%. This does not establish that a walking intervention inevitably reduces mortality by over 50%, that more steps are always better, or an independent cadence benefit.
walking-steps.population: CARDIA: 2,110 Black/White US adults, mean age 45.2; 10.8 years follow-up, 72 deaths
walking-steps.design: Single prospective cohort with accelerometer measurements
walking-steps.gradeReason: Direct ACM, but few deaths and unstable single-cohort estimates
walking-steps.limitations: Short-term activity measurement; residual confounding and reverse causation; 7,000 steps is not a universal threshold.
walking-steps.action: Gradually increase walking from your own baseline; individualize for mobility limitations, fall risk or cardiopulmonary disease.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract Results: n=2,110, 72 deaths; moderate HR 0.28 (0.15–0.54), high HR 0.45 (0.25–0.81); cadence was not significantly associated after adjustment.

toothbrushing.originalClaim: People who rarely brush have 9%, 12% and 25% higher risks of cancer, COPD and cirrhosis, and 25% higher premature mortality; the action section states brushing gives −25% ACM.
toothbrushing.finding: Rarely/never brushing versus regular brushing had ACM HR 1.25; the cancer, COPD and cirrhosis figures mainly concern incidence. This observation does not mean starting to brush reduces ACM by 25%, nor establish a causal effect of the toothbrush itself.
toothbrushing.gradeReason: Large cohort with direct ACM and adjustment for multiple confounders; not intervention evidence
toothbrushing.limitations: Self-reported brushing; related to smoking, poverty, prior health and access to care.
toothbrushing.action: Brush regularly with fluoride toothpaste and obtain dental care; this does not replace smoking control, blood pressure management or similar measures.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract Results: 9.3% rarely/never brushed; ACM 1.25 (1.21–1.28), cancer 1.09 (1.04–1.14), COPD 1.12 (1.05–1.20), cirrhosis 1.25 (1.09–1.44).

tub-bathing.originalClaim: Daily tub bathing versus 1–2 times/week or none: 28% lower CVD risk, 26% lower stroke risk, 46% lower intracerebral hemorrhage risk; no association with increased sudden death.
tub-bathing.finding: The original 28%, 26% and 46% correspond to incident CVD, stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage; the figures are verifiable but do not concern ACM. No significant sudden-death association does not establish complete bathing safety.
tub-bathing.effect: ACM not reported; incident CVD HR 0.72
tub-bathing.ci: ACM not reported; incident CVD 95% CI 0.62–0.84
tub-bathing.comparison: Almost daily/daily tub bathing versus 0–2 times/week
tub-bathing.population: 30,076 Japanese people aged 40–59, no baseline CVD or cancer; follow-up 1990–2009
tub-bathing.design: Japanese prospective cohort; cardiovascular/cerebrovascular event endpoints
tub-bathing.gradeReason: Indirect evidence with non-ACM endpoints for this entry
tub-bathing.limitations: Nonrandomized; Japanese tub-bathing habits cannot directly be generalized to showers; a nonsignificant sudden-death finding does not exclude drowning, heat stress or other risks.
tub-bathing.action: Bathe in comfortably warm water with safe habits. Avoid prolonged hot or solitary baths with fainting tendency, acute illness, alcohol use or unstable cardiovascular disease.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: 2,097 CVD events; CVD HR 0.72 (0.62–0.84), stroke 0.74 (0.62–0.87), intracerebral hemorrhage 0.54 (0.40–0.73); no sudden-death association found.

heavy-housework.originalClaim: Men doing heavy housework weekly after age 72 can reduce average mortality by 29%.
heavy-housework.finding: Heavy-housework participation in men was associated with 29% lower ACM, but 72 was the sample mean age; eligibility was age ≥65. This does not mean benefits begin only after 72 or represent a trial reducing “average mortality.” Results in women were nonsignificant.
heavy-housework.population: Community-dwelling Hong Kong adults aged ≥65; 2,867 after excluding specified chronic diseases, mean age 72; 452 deaths
heavy-housework.design: Single prospective cohort, about 9 years follow-up
heavy-housework.gradeReason: Direct ACM but single cohort and sex stratification; substantial confounding by physical capability
heavy-housework.limitations: People able to do housework may already be healthier; moving furniture/gas cylinders is not a longevity prescription. The 2013 correction only fixes male/female housework participation proportions.
heavy-housework.action: Do suitable housework within your capacity; avoid heavy lifting with frailty, osteoporosis, back problems or fall risk.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract/Results: after further adjustment for BMI, frailty, living arrangement and leisure activity, male ACM HR 0.71 (0.56–0.91); no significant association in women. Correction PMC3825706 revises housework participation to 52–81% for men and 64–93% for women.

sleep-duration.originalClaim: Mortality is lowest at 7 hours; compared with 7 hours, ≥10 hours gives 34% higher ACM in men and 48% in women.
sleep-duration.finding: The figures match: versus self-reported 7 hours, ≥10 hours was associated with 34% higher ACM in men and 48% in women. Long sleep may reflect underlying disease; this does not justify forcing long sleepers down to 7 hours or asserting that changing duration inevitably changes mortality.
sleep-duration.comparison: Self-reported ≥10 hours versus 7 hours; cohorts measured either nighttime sleep or total daily sleep including naps
sleep-duration.population: 9 cohorts in Japan, China, Singapore and Korea: 322,721 people, mean age 54.5; excluded baseline self-reported CVD/cancer and deaths within the first 5 years; 19,419 male and 13,768 female deaths
sleep-duration.design: Pooled individual-participant data from multiple cohorts; prospective follow-up about 13–14 years
sleep-duration.gradeReason: Direct ACM across multiple cohorts with a consistent J-shaped association; noncausal
sleep-duration.limitations: Sleep duration was self-reported once: at baseline in most cohorts and at the third follow-up in the Shanghai Women’s Health Study; questionnaires not standardized across cohorts (nighttime or total daily sleep including naps); residual confounding and no information on sleep quality, depression, socioeconomic status and similar factors. Excluding baseline CVD/cancer and early 5-year deaths cannot fully eliminate reverse causation.
sleep-duration.action: Maintain sufficient, regular and restorative sleep. Persistent long sleep with fatigue, snoring or sleepiness warrants investigation.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract/All-Cause Mortality: ≥10 hours, multivariable-adjusted men 1.34 (1.26–1.44), women 1.48 (1.36–1.61); reference 7 hours; Methods exclude deaths within the first 5 years.

bedtime.originalClaim: 22:00–24:00 is best; early bedtime increases ACM by 43%, late bedtime by 15%; the original notes controversy.
bedtime.finding: The original study verifies associations of early/late bedtime with adverse outcomes, but the original-paper abstract read does not give separate effects and CIs for “43%/15% higher ACM.” Secondary figures cannot be copied as fully adjusted ACM. Fully adjusted abstract results are HR 1.09 and 1.10 for the death + nonfatal cardiovascular event composite, not pure ACM.
bedtime.effect: Separate ACM figures unverified; composite endpoint HR 1.09/1.10
bedtime.comparison: Before about 22:00 or after midnight versus 22:00 to midnight
bedtime.population: PURE: 112,198 people in 21 countries; 9.2 years; 5,633 deaths, 5,346 major cardiovascular events
bedtime.gradeReason: Original paper includes mortality follow-up, but only the abstract was read this round and separate ACM estimates were not rechecked; composite endpoints cannot be upgraded to ACM evidence
bedtime.limitations: Social schedules and disease confounding; full adjustment markedly attenuated associations. Exact boundaries differ slightly between Methods and Conclusion and should not be hard thresholds.
bedtime.action: Keep regular, adequate sleep according to your own rhythm; this association does not justify deliberately delaying an otherwise suitable early bedtime.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Results: age/sex-adjusted composite endpoint 1.29 (1.22–1.35), 1.11 (1.03–1.20); fully adjusted 1.09 (1.03–1.16), 1.10 (1.02–1.20). Original secondary 43%/15% retained as unverified ACM.

sedentary-time.originalClaim: Each additional sedentary hour increases CVD incidence risk by 4%, cancer by 1% and ACM by 3%; thresholds are 6–8 hours/day for total sitting and 3–4 hours/day for TV.
sedentary-time.finding: Higher sedentary time is associated with higher ACM, but a fixed 3% per additional hour does not apply at every level. The corresponding systematic review found nonlinearity: about 1% per hour at total sedentary time ≤8 hours and about 4% above 8 hours; television viewing also has different slopes. The 6–8-hour and 3–4-hour points are observational-model inflections, not safety limits.
sedentary-time.effect: RR per additional 1 hour of total sedentary time 1.01 (≤8 h/day); 1.04 (>8 h/day)
sedentary-time.comparison: An additional 1 hour/day of total sedentary time within each exposure interval
sedentary-time.population: 34 prospective studies; 1,331,468 unique participants across different outcomes
sedentary-time.design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis, adjusted for physical activity
sedentary-time.gradeReason: Pooled direct ACM from multiple cohorts; not a randomized intervention
sedentary-time.limitations: Mostly self-reported sitting, heterogeneity and residual confounding. Cancer mortality was not significantly associated in this review and must not be confused with cancer incidence. Original Chinese report PDF and old WHO PDF were inaccessible.
sedentary-time.action: Replace some sitting with movement or activity within your abilities and exercise regularly. If unable to stand, follow rehabilitation guidance; no unproven universal break frequency is prescribed.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract: PA-adjusted total sedentary ACM RR/hour 1.01 (1.00–1.01) at ≤8 h and 1.04 (1.03–1.05) at >8 h; TV 1.03 (1.01–1.04) at ≤3.5 h and 1.06 (1.05–1.08) at >3.5 h.

pessimism.originalClaim: Each 1 SD of pessimism is associated with ACM HR 1.134 and cardiovascular mortality HR 1.196; optimism was not significantly associated. The original calls reverse causation “impossible.”
pessimism.finding: The original HR 1.134 and related figures match the paper and refer to each 1 SD higher pessimism score. Nonsignificant optimism findings do not prove optimism is unhelpful; the paper’s description of reverse causation as “unlikely” does not exclude it.
pessimism.effect: ACM HR 1.134 per 1 SD of pessimism; further-adjusted HR 1.160
pessimism.population: Australian twin-related sample aged ≥50: 2,978 people, 1,068 deaths after about 20 years; model samples smaller owing to missing data
pessimism.design: Single prospective cohort; survival models account for family clustering
pessimism.gradeReason: Direct ACM but single cohort with substantial personality/health confounding
pessimism.limitations: Psychological traits not randomized; reverse causation not excluded; no direct trial evidence of emotional treatment reducing ACM.
pessimism.action: Seek support or professional help when persistent pessimism or low mood affects life; forced optimism does not replace treatment.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract and Table 1: age-adjusted score with sex in the model, ACM HR 1.134 (1.065–1.207); adding BMI, alcohol and smoking, HR 1.160 (1.083–1.242); optimism not significantly associated.

wealth.originalClaim: 5,414 middle-aged adults (mean 46.7 years): higher net worth is associated with longevity, with a similar direction among 2,490 siblings and twins.
wealth.finding: The original sample and direction match. Per additional US$50,000 net worth, ACM HR was 0.95 and within-family HR 0.94, but the twin-only subgroup CI crossed 1. This does not show that a particular investment extends life proportionally through wealth gains, nor describe an ecological effect of wealth inequality.
wealth.effect: HR 0.95 per additional US$50,000 net worth; within-family HR 0.94
wealth.comparison: Each additional US$50,000 in self-reported 1994–1996 net worth (study unit)
wealth.population: US MIDUS: 5,414 people, mean age 46.7, nearly 24 years follow-up; 1,010 deaths; 2,490 siblings/twins
wealth.gradeReason: Direct ACM and family comparisons, but single cohort with incompletely controlled economic/health confounding
wealth.limitations: Self-reported net worth; limited demographic representation; individual nonshared confounding and health-related wealth loss; no income-improvement intervention tested.
wealth.action: Prioritize stable housing, access to care and basic financial security; high-risk investment is not a health intervention.

sources.evidence: Author research-project archived full text, Results/Table 2: full sample HR 0.95 (0.94–0.97) per $50,000; within-family 0.94 (0.91–0.97); identical twins alone 0.95 (0.87–1.04).

weight-change.factor: Weight change from early adulthood to midlife
weight-change.originalClaim: Obesity to overweight versus persistent obesity gives 54% lower ACM (HR 0.46); overweight to normal showed no decrease (HR 1.12). The action section abbreviates this as weight loss −54%.
weight-change.finding: Obesity to overweight versus persistent obesity HR 0.46 matches. Overweight to normal versus persistent overweight HR 1.12 has a CI crossing 1: no significant difference, not proof that reaching normal weight is unhelpful or harmful. Weight loss occurred between age 25 and midlife, not involuntary weight loss in old age.
weight-change.comparison: Versus persistent obesity and persistent overweight, respectively
weight-change.population: NHANES: 24,205 US adults aged 40–74; recalled weights at age 25 and 10 years before baseline; 10.7 years follow-up, 5,846 deaths
weight-change.design: Observational recalled weight history linked to prospective mortality
weight-change.gradeReason: Direct ACM but recall bias, small weight-loss sample and inability to distinguish intention or causes
weight-change.limitations: Only 214 people changed from obese to overweight; nonrandomized; no proof of a causal 54% benefit from intentional loss.
weight-change.action: People with obesity should plan long-term weight and muscle-strength management with health professionals. Do not transfer these conclusions to older age, pregnancy or involuntary weight loss.

sources.evidence: Full text, Abstract and Table 3: obese-overweight versus obese-obese 0.46 (0.27–0.77); overweight-normal versus overweight-overweight 1.12 (0.86–1.45); Table 1: 214 obese→overweight participants.

covid-pandemic.factor: COVID-19 pandemic and all-cause excess deaths
covid-pandemic.originalClaim: US COVID mortality is about 1.5%, with a 2-year reduction in life expectancy; the cited paper’s title concerns first-wave ACM in 21 industrialized countries.
covid-pandemic.finding: The original paper supports first-wave all-cause excess deaths, but its 21 countries comprise 19 European countries plus Australia and New Zealand, excluding the US. It cannot support the original “1.5% US COVID mortality” or “2-year life expectancy reduction”; the former also lacks a date, denominator and case/infection fatality definition. Pandemic excess deaths include indirect effects such as disrupted care.
covid-pandemic.effect: 206,000 excess deaths in 21 countries from mid-February to late May 2020; not an individual HR
covid-pandemic.ci: 95% Bayesian credible interval 178,100–231,000; not a 95% confidence interval
covid-pandemic.comparison: Observed all-cause deaths versus modeled counterfactual without the pandemic
covid-pandemic.population: National death registries in 21 industrialized countries, first wave of 2020; excludes the US
covid-pandemic.design: Population time-series/ecological study using an ensemble of 16 Bayesian models
covid-pandemic.gradeReason: Direct ACM totals, but ecological data cannot estimate an individual infection’s ACM effect
covid-pandemic.limitations: Counterfactual models and registration delays; the 2020 setting cannot be extrapolated to current variants, immunity and care. Original CDC link is a general mortality-data portal, not direct support for the original figures.
covid-pandemic.action: Reduce infection exposure and maintain chronic-disease care and timely medical access. Follow currently applicable prevention/treatment guidance rather than estimating personal risk from fixed 2020 percentages.

sources.evidence: Original PDF full text, Abstract, Results and Table 1: 206,000 excess deaths in 21 countries (95% credible interval 178,100–231,000); Introduction specifies 19 European countries + Australia/New Zealand; not US infection fatality or life expectancy estimates.

resistance-training.originalClaim: New factor; the original repository had no corresponding figures.
resistance-training.finding: A meta-analysis of prospective cohorts associated any muscle-strengthening activity versus none with about 15% lower ACM. The curve suggested larger benefits around 30–60 minutes/week, but high-dose effects are uncertain; this is not an optimal dose confirmed by randomized trials.
resistance-training.comparison: Any muscle-strengthening activity versus none, adjusting for aerobic activity where possible
resistance-training.population: Binary ACM synthesis: 7 studies, 263,058 people, 42,133 deaths; 16 studies in the overall review
resistance-training.gradeReason: Direct ACM synthesis with consistent direction across cohorts; project grade B is not the paper’s GRADE, which rated ACM certainty very low
resistance-training.limitations: I²=83%; self-report, healthy-participant bias and confounding; the J-shaped curve does not establish that more training is harmful.
resistance-training.action: If physically able, gradually train major muscle groups alongside aerobic activity. Pain, recent surgery or unstable chronic disease require prior assessment and adjustment.

sources.evidence: Full text, Table 1 and All-cause mortality: 7 studies, 42,133/263,058 deaths/participants, RR 0.85 (0.79–0.93), I² 83%; each study RR<1; original GRADE: very low.

social-isolation.factor: Social isolation, loneliness and living alone
social-isolation.originalClaim: New factor; the original repository had no corresponding figures.
social-isolation.finding: Adjusted meta-analytic results associate social isolation, loneliness and living alone with mortality odds ratios of 1.29, 1.26 and 1.32, respectively. These are distinct exposures; OR cannot be rewritten as HR or an increase in individual absolute mortality. It is unproven that increased social contact necessarily reverses risk by the same magnitude.
social-isolation.effect: Social isolation OR 1.29; loneliness OR 1.26; living alone OR 1.32
social-isolation.ci: Not reported (the original abstract read gives no 95% CI; none added from secondary sources)
social-isolation.comparison: Social isolation/loneliness/living alone versus the corresponding lower-exposure group in each study
social-isolation.population: Mortality follow-up studies through February 2014; populations and adjustments differ across studies
social-isolation.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of original studies
social-isolation.gradeReason: Multiple-study synthesis with direct mortality endpoints; noninterventional and noncausal
social-isolation.limitations: Baseline health affects results; heterogeneous exposure definitions; living alone is not loneliness; abstract only in this review round.
social-isolation.action: Maintain reliable contacts and ways to seek help according to personal wishes; address hearing, mobility, depression and similar barriers. Not everyone living alone needs to cohabit.

sources.evidence: Abstract reports adjusted social isolation OR 1.29, loneliness OR 1.26 and living alone OR 1.32; baseline health affects results; no CIs listed.

intensive-bp-control.factor: Intensive blood pressure control in eligible people
intensive-bp-control.originalClaim: New factor; the original repository had no corresponding figures.
intensive-bp-control.finding: In SPRINT participants without diabetes and at increased cardiovascular risk, a systolic target <120 versus <140 mmHg reduced ACM by about 27%. This is a treatment-strategy trial, not evidence that antihypertensives extend life in every healthy person; CVD composite HR 0.75 and ACM HR 0.73 are separately reported.
intensive-bp-control.comparison: Intensive systolic target <120 versus standard target <140 mmHg
intensive-bp-control.population: 9,361 adults with SBP ≥130 mmHg, increased cardiovascular risk and no diabetes
intensive-bp-control.design: SPRINT randomized controlled trial; median follow-up 3.26 years, stopped early
intensive-bp-control.gradeReason: Direct randomized ACM comparison; clearly defined applicability, retaining early-stopping and adverse-event limitations
intensive-bp-control.limitations: Early stopping may overestimate benefit; hypotension, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities and acute kidney injury were more common; not generalizable to diabetes or low-risk normotensive people.
intensive-bp-control.action: With diagnosed hypertension and higher risk, discuss targets with a clinician and monitor kidney function, electrolytes and postural symptoms. Do not independently add medication or pursue the trial target.

sources.evidence: Abstract, Methods/Results: n=9,361; ACM HR 0.73 (0.60–0.90), P=.003; primary CVD composite 0.75 (0.64–0.89); more serious hypotension, syncope, electrolyte and renal adverse events in the intensive group.

cardiorespiratory-fitness.originalClaim: New entry; the original repository did not separately list cardiorespiratory fitness.
cardiorespiratory-fitness.finding: Each 1 MET higher cardiorespiratory fitness measured by exercise testing is associated with lower ACM. This is an observational association with physical capacity, not a guaranteed benefit of “exercising 1 MET more.”
cardiorespiratory-fitness.comparison: Each 1 MET higher CRF; not a comparison of exercise minutes
cardiorespiratory-fitness.population: 34 adult cohorts in the review; continuous-dose ACM analysis uses a subset
cardiorespiratory-fitness.gradeReason: Pooled cohorts with relatively objective measurement, but association alone cannot establish the causal effect of changing fitness.
cardiorespiratory-fitness.limitations: Very high heterogeneity; prior disease, genetics and test protocols affect CRF; search through 2019-12-26.
cardiorespiratory-fitness.action: Use fitness as a clue in physical-capacity assessment and train gradually according to baseline health; do not directly use RR to estimate personal life extension.

sources.evidence: Europe PMC abstract, Results: ACM RR 0.88 (0.83–0.93) per 1 MET; original-text search excerpt indicates I²=99.4% for this analysis.

dapagliflozin-ckd.originalClaim: New entry; the original repository did not list SGLT2 inhibitors.
dapagliflozin-ckd.finding: In people with CKD meeting DAPA-CKD eligibility, the randomized treatment group had lower ACM. This is not evidence for anti-aging medication in healthy people.
dapagliflozin-ckd.comparison: Dapagliflozin 10 mg/day versus placebo, both on standard care
dapagliflozin-ckd.population: 4,304 adults with CKD; eGFR 25–75, UACR 200–5,000 mg/g; median follow-up 2.4 years; with/without type 2 diabetes
dapagliflozin-ckd.design: Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial; ACM a prespecified key secondary endpoint
dapagliflozin-ckd.gradeReason: Random allocation and direct ACM recording; main limits are population applicability and early stopping.
dapagliflozin-ckd.limitations: Stopped early for efficacy; not generalizable to healthy people without CKD, type 1 diabetes or excluded kidney diseases. The 4.7%/6.8% are trial-period death proportions, not lifetime risk.
dapagliflozin-ckd.action: A clinician should assess CKD and other indications, considering volume depletion, infection, ketoacidosis and other risks. Dose describes the trial regimen only.

sources.evidence: Abstract/Methods/Results and Table 2: ACM prespecified secondary endpoint, 101/2,152 versus 146/2,152; HR 0.69 (0.53–0.88); median 2.4 years.

semaglutide-select.originalClaim: New entry; the original repository did not list GLP-1 receptor agonists.
semaglutide-select.finding: SELECT’s ACM estimate favored lower mortality, but the main trial’s hierarchical testing did not pass cardiovascular death. ACM therefore cannot be treated as confirmatory superiority under multiplicity control.
semaglutide-select.comparison: Subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly versus placebo, on standard care
semaglutide-select.population: 17,604 people; age ≥45, BMI ≥27, established cardiovascular disease, no diabetes; mean follow-up 39.8 months
semaglutide-select.design: Randomized double-blind trial and its mortality-outcome analysis
semaglutide-select.gradeReason: Randomized evidence, downgraded because the ACM hierarchical test was not completed; grade B here does not mean observational research.
semaglutide-select.limitations: Not generalizable to younger people, those without cardiovascular disease or those with normal BMI; manufacturer funded; adverse-event discontinuation in the main trial 16.6% versus 8.2%.
semaglutide-select.action: Assess only under relevant clinical indications; exploratory ACM findings are not a longevity promise for healthy people.

sources.evidence: Efficacy End Points: CV death did not meet the hierarchical threshold, so subsequent ACM superiority testing was not performed; Europe PMC abstract reports discontinuation 16.6% versus 8.2%. Original-site full-text request returned 403; full-text reading is not claimed.

aspirin-primary-prevention.originalClaim: New counterexample; preventive medication cannot be assumed to extend life.
aspirin-primary-prevention.finding: ASPREE did not support starting daily aspirin for longevity in older people without prior cardiovascular disease. The secondary ACM endpoint signaled higher mortality, but without multiple-comparison adjustment and requiring cautious interpretation.
aspirin-primary-prevention.population: 19,114 community-dwelling older adults, generally ≥70 (Black/Hispanic US participants ≥65), without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability; median 4.7 years
aspirin-primary-prevention.design: Randomized double-blind trial; ACM secondary endpoint
aspirin-primary-prevention.gradeReason: Randomized direct ACM evidence, but secondary-outcome multiplicity and an unexpected cancer-death signal limit certainty.
aspirin-primary-prevention.limitations: Not fully consistent with previous studies; not applicable to secondary prevention after myocardial infarction/stroke; does not mean aspirin raises ACM at every age.
aspirin-primary-prevention.action: Do not independently start aspirin solely for longevity. If taking it for a clear indication, discuss with a clinician rather than stopping on the basis of this trial.

sources.evidence: Results: 1,052 deaths; ACM 12.7 versus 11.1 per 1,000 person-years, HR 1.14 (1.01–1.29).
Discussion explicitly states that CIs were not adjusted for multiple secondary endpoints; the authors urge cautious interpretation of higher ACM.

walking-steps-2025.originalClaim: Adds pooled multiple-cohort evidence beyond the original single-cohort step-count entry.
walking-steps-2025.finding: The 2025 review abstract associates 7,000 versus 2,000 steps/day with lower ACM. The between-group association cannot directly be treated as a personal intervention benefit of increasing from 2,000 to 7,000 steps.
walking-steps-2025.population: Adult prospective cohorts; 14 studies in this ACM comparison; review search through 2025-02-14
walking-steps-2025.gradeReason: Device-measured direct ACM synthesis across multiple cohorts; authors’ GRADE moderate certainty is not the project’s causal certainty.
walking-steps-2025.limitations: Residual confounding; no age-stratified conclusions; differences in devices, measurement periods and prior disease. Based on abstract figures this round, without table-by-table full-text review.
walking-steps-2025.action: Increase steps within your ability; 7,000 can be a gradual target for some people, not a mandatory threshold for everyone.

sources.evidence: Findings: 14 ACM studies; 7,000 versus 2,000 steps HR 0.53 (0.46–0.60), I²=36.3%; authors’ ACM GRADE: moderate.

metformin-adverse-events.factor: Metformin adverse reactions (checking denominators and definitions)
metformin-adverse-events.originalClaim: Vitamin B12 deficiency 7%–17.4%; gastrointestinal adverse reactions up to 53%; fatigue 9%, headache 6%; rare serious lactic acidosis and liver injury.
metformin-adverse-events.finding: The US label’s 53% refers to diarrhea in a specific trial; 9% asthenia and 6% headache also come from that trial, not general rates in everyone taking metformin. About 7% in a 29-week trial developed below-normal serum B12, not necessarily symptomatic deficiency; the 17.4% upper value was not verified from this label. Lactic acidosis has a boxed warning; liver injury is a postmarketing report, and spontaneous reports cannot estimate frequency.
metformin-adverse-events.effect: ACM effect not assessed; diarrhea 53% versus 12%
metformin-adverse-events.ci: ACM not reported; adverse-reaction intervals not listed
metformin-adverse-events.comparison: Immediate-release metformin tablets versus placebo; up to 2,550 mg/day
metformin-adverse-events.population: US type 2 diabetes trial in the label: 141 treated, 145 placebo; B12 data from a 29-week trial
metformin-adverse-events.design: Official drug-label adverse-reaction trial data and postmarketing reports; not an ACM intervention study
metformin-adverse-events.gradeReason: Clear safety source, but only indirect for longevity/ACM; D does not dispute drug-label reliability.
metformin-adverse-events.limitations: Reaction rates across formulations, titration, doses, follow-up and populations are not directly comparable; no uniform definition supplied for 17.4%; adverse-reaction frequencies are not mortality risks.
metformin-adverse-events.action: Use according to clinical indications and monitor kidney function and B12; this entry corrects frequency definitions and denominators, not a basis for independently starting or stopping treatment.

sources.evidence: Label updated 2026-06: Table 1, diarrhea 53%/12%, asthenia 9%/6%, headache 6%/5%; section 5.2, about 7% developed low serum B12. Section 6.2 liver injury is from spontaneous reports.

waist-circumference.originalClaim: Added: consider abdominal fat distribution alongside body weight.
waist-circumference.finding: Pooled prospective adult cohorts associated each 10 cm larger waist with about 11% higher all-cause mortality risk. Central fat measures provided additional risk information after accounting for BMI.
waist-circumference.comparison: Per 10 cm larger waist; comparison across adults with different waist sizes
waist-circumference.population: Review: 72 prospective cohorts, 2,528,297 participants; waist analysis: 50 studies
waist-circumference.design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts
waist-circumference.gradeReason: Direct ACM evidence across multiple cohorts; observational studies do not quantify a personal treatment benefit from reducing waist size.
waist-circumference.limitations: Substantial between-study heterogeneity; differences in waist measurement, existing illness and lifestyle. Waist size is a risk marker, not a direct measurement of visceral fat; this finding does not define a universal weight-loss target.
waist-circumference.action: Track waist changes alongside weight; if abdominal fat is increasing, work on food, activity and a health assessment.

sources.evidence: Abstract Results: 72 cohorts overall; waist analysis included 50 studies, with HR 1.11 (95% CI 1.08–1.13) per 10 cm larger waist; associations persisted after accounting for BMI.

obstructive-sleep-apnoea.originalClaim: Added: consider repeated pauses in breathing during sleep and their health effects.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.finding: Pooled prospective observational studies linked severe obstructive sleep apnoea with higher all-cause mortality. In a 2025 treatment review, pooled randomised trials did not show a clear reduction in ACM with positive airway pressure, while non-randomised studies found lower risk.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.effect: Severe vs no sleep apnoea: HR 1.90
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.comparison: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea vs no disease; not treatment vs no treatment
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.population: Risk review: 6 prospective observational studies, 11,932 people, grouped by apnoea severity
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.design: Meta-analysis of prospective observational studies; additional synthesis of positive airway pressure treatment studies
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.gradeReason: Direct ACM association across multiple cohorts; this grade concerns disease-related risk, not a proven mortality reduction from treatment.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.limitations: Existing illness and treatment selection may influence results. The treatment review combines randomised and non-randomised studies, so its pooled result is not wholly randomised evidence. Snoring alone is not a diagnosis.
obstructive-sleep-apnoea.action: Seek a sleep assessment for persistent loud snoring, breathing pauses during sleep or ongoing daytime sleepiness; discuss treatment if diagnosed.

sources.evidence: Abstract Results: 6 studies, 11,932 participants; severe OSA all-cause mortality HR 1.90 (95% CI 1.29–2.81).
Full-text Results: 30 studies, including 10 randomised and 20 non-randomised studies; RCT-only ACM HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.65–1.16), non-randomised-only HR 0.60 (0.52–0.70).
Symptoms page: breathing that starts and stops, frequent loud snoring and daytime sleepiness; these warrant discussion with a health professional.

hepatitis-c-treatment.factor: Finding and treating chronic hepatitis C
hepatitis-c-treatment.originalClaim: Added: consider testing and antiviral treatment for people with chronic hepatitis C infection.
hepatitis-c-treatment.finding: In a French prospective cohort of people with chronic hepatitis C, direct-acting antiviral treatment was associated with about 52% lower adjusted all-cause mortality risk. Participants had established infection, and treatment was not randomly assigned.
hepatitis-c-treatment.comparison: Direct-acting antiviral treatment vs no treatment in chronic hepatitis C; time-varying treatment exposure
hepatitis-c-treatment.population: 9,895 adults with chronic hepatitis C at 32 French liver centres; median follow-up 33.4 months
hepatitis-c-treatment.design: Prospective multicentre observational cohort with time-dependent modelling and adjustment for confounders
hepatitis-c-treatment.gradeReason: Direct ACM outcome from a single observational cohort; treatment-selection and other confounding may remain after adjustment.
hepatitis-c-treatment.limitations: The study excluded people with prior decompensated cirrhosis, liver cancer or liver transplantation, among others. It does not apply to uninfected people and is not a randomised comparison of regimens. A positive antibody test alone does not confirm current infection.
hepatitis-c-treatment.action: After a positive hepatitis C antibody test, check whether the virus is still present. If current infection is confirmed, get a liver assessment and discuss antiviral treatment.

sources.evidence: Abstract: 9,895 participants; median follow-up 33.4 months; adjusted all-cause mortality HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.33–0.70) for antiviral exposure.
Testing guidance: a reactive antibody test needs an HCV RNA test to identify current infection; positive RNA results should lead to care and treatment.
